lead: A sandwich panel is two thin stiff sheets, the faces, glued to a thick light core. The faces carry tension and compression like the flanges of an I-beam; the core carries shear and holds the faces apart. Spacing the faces out multiplies the bending stiffness while adding little weight. Aircraft use sandwich panels for floor panels, control surfaces such as ailerons and rudders, radomes and helicopter rotor blades. This chapter shows why the arrangement is stiff, what the core looks like, how the panel is glued, and how it fails.
prereq: You need: Structural components of aircraft and their functions for the idea of a load path, Typical wing and fuselage structures for the skin-stringer panels that sandwich panels partly replace, and simple bending stress and second moment of area, which return in full with the bending of thin-walled beams.

blocks.text: Bend a solid sheet of thickness t and its bending stiffness per unit width is D = E t³/12. Doubling t makes it eight times stiffer and twice as heavy. Most material in a solid sheet sits near the neutral axis and does little work.

A sandwich panel moves material away from the neutral axis. Two faces of thickness t<sub>f</sub> are bonded to a core, and their mid-planes are a distance d apart. Per unit width each face has area t<sub>f</sub> and sits at d/2 from the neutral axis, so I = 2 × t<sub>f</sub> × (d/2)² = t<sub>f</sub> d²/2.

blocks.where: D is the bending stiffness per unit width, in N·m; E<sub>f</sub> is Young's modulus of the face material, in Pa; t<sub>f</sub> is the face thickness, in m; d is the distance between the face mid-planes, in m, roughly the core thickness plus one face thickness.

blocks.text: Each face also bends about its own mid-plane, adding E<sub>f</sub> t<sub>f</sub>³/12, but t<sub>f</sub> is a fraction of a millimetre while d is tens of millimetres, so that term is dropped.

The faces act like I-beam flanges, one in compression and one in tension, a couple separated by d. The core acts like the web, carrying the transverse shear that comes with bending, and keeps the faces flat so the compressed face cannot buckle early.
The core is the thick, light middle. Three families cover most aircraft work.

items: Hexagonal honeycomb. Thin foil or paper is formed into half-hexagons, stacked and glued at the node lines, then pulled open into cells. Aluminium honeycomb is stiff and cheap. Nomex honeycomb, aramid paper coated with phenolic resin, resists fire and moisture. Panels are much stiffer along the ribbon direction, the direction the foil runs, so drawings must state the orientation.

Foam. Closed-cell PVC and polyurethane foams are cheap; polymethacrylimide foam costs much more but is stiffer and tolerates higher cure temperatures. All work about equally in both in-plane directions and machine easily. For the same weight they carry less shear than honeycomb.
Balsa. End-grain wood, still used in some rotor blades and boat hulls.

blocks.text: The adhesive matters as much as the core. A film adhesive is laid between face and core and cured under heat and pressure, in an autoclave, a press or a vacuum bag. The glue line must be continuous. A void, a greasy patch or trapped moisture is a crack waiting to run.
A sandwich panel is stiff and strong but not tough. The designer checks each failure mode; the weakest sets the allowable load.

items: Face yielding. The face stress reaches the yield stress of the face material. Rarely the critical mode.

Face wrinkling. The compressed face buckles into the core over a short wavelength set by the face bending stiffness and the core stiffness, often only a few times the face thickness. Soft cores allow this well below yield.
Core shear. The core carries the shear force, mainly through cell walls aligned with the shear. Its shear strength is low, so shear often governs short, deep panels.
Core crushing. A local load, a jack, a bolt or a foot, crushes the cells. Honeycomb is weak in this through-thickness direction.
Debonding. The face lifts off the core. The faces then work alone, stiffness collapses and failure can be sudden. Bad surface preparation, moisture or a poor cure causes it.

blocks.text: Bolts are a special problem: a bolt through a sandwich crushes the core, so holes are potted with a solid insert before drilling. A sandwich does the job of a skin-and-stringer panel with the material pushed to the outside.

spec.aria: Cross-section of a sandwich panel: two thin aluminium faces, 0.5 millimetres each, on a 20 millimetre honeycomb core, with the 20.5 millimetre distance between the face mid-planes marked. Arrows show compression in the top face and tension in the bottom face. Two boxes compare bending stiffness: 7354 newton metres per metre for the sandwich against 5.83 for a solid 1.0 millimetre sheet.

examples.question: An aircraft floor panel has two aluminium faces, each 0.5 mm thick with E = 70 GPa, bonded to a 20 mm honeycomb core. (a) Find the bending stiffness D per metre width. (b) A solid aluminium sheet of the same mass per unit area, with the core weight neglected, is 1.0 mm thick. Find its D and the ratio of the two stiffnesses.
steps: Convert to metres: t<sub>f</sub> = 0.5 mm = 0.5 × 10⁻³ m; core thickness = 20 mm = 0.020 m; E<sub>f</sub> = 70 GPa = 70 × 10⁹ Pa.
Distance between face mid-planes: d = 0.020 + 0.0005 = 0.0205 m.
Halve it: D = 7.354 × 10³ N·m = 7.35 kN·m per metre width.
Equal-mass solid sheet: 2 × 0.5 mm = 1.0 mm = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m. D = E t³/12 = 70 × 10⁹ × (1.0 × 10⁻³)³ / 12 = 5.83 N·m per metre width.
examples.answer: The sandwich panel has D = 7.35 kN·m per metre width against 5.83 N·m for the equal-mass solid sheet, so the sandwich is about 1261 times stiffer in bending.
examples.check:
E = 70e9
t = 0.5e-3
d = 20e-3 + t
D = E*t*d**2/2
print(round(D, 3))
t<sub>solid</sub> = 2*t
D<sub>solid</sub> = E*t<sub>solid</sub>**3/12
print(round(D<sub>solid</sub>, 3))
print(round(D/D<sub>solid</sub>, 2))

examples.question: A designer keeps the same 0.5 mm aluminium faces (E = 70 GPa) but doubles the core from 10 mm to 20 mm. By what factor does D rise?
steps: Second panel: d₂ = 0.0205 m, D₂ = 7354 N·m per metre width, from the first example.
The face mass per unit area is unchanged, but the core mass doubles. The core is light, so the total panel weight rises only modestly.
examples.answer: D rises by a factor of 3.81, from 1.93 kN·m to 7.35 kN·m per metre width. The gain comes for a modest rise in panel weight, not for zero weight.

traps: Quoting only the faces' own bending stiffness, 2 × E<sub>f</sub> t<sub>f</sub>³/12, and forgetting the d² term. That d² term is what the whole idea is about.
Using the core thickness as d and forgetting to add one face thickness. With 20 mm core and 0.5 mm faces, d is 20.5 mm, not 20 mm.
Checking face stress only. Core shear and debonding are common critical modes, and a panel that passes the face check can still fail in service.
Treating honeycomb as isotropic. Stiffness and shear strength differ strongly between the ribbon direction and across it, so orientation must be specified.
Mixing units: putting t<sub>f</sub> in millimetres into a formula where E is in Pa and d is in metres. The answer comes out a thousand times wrong.

quiz.q: Name the three parts of a sandwich panel and say what each carries in bending.
quiz.a: Two face sheets, which carry the bending tension and compression like I-beam flanges, and a core, which carries the transverse shear like the web and holds the faces apart. Adhesive layers join them.

quiz.q: Name three core materials used in aircraft sandwich panels.
quiz.a: Aluminium honeycomb, Nomex (aramid paper) honeycomb and closed-cell foam; balsa is a fourth.

quiz.q: Why does the face separation d enter the stiffness as d² and not as d?
quiz.a: Each face of area t<sub>f</sub> sits at d/2 from the neutral axis, and second moment of area uses distance squared: t<sub>f</sub> (d/2)² per face. Two faces give t<sub>f</sub> d²/2, so the stiffness grows with the square of the separation.

quiz.q: A compressed sandwich face and a plain sheet of the same thickness both buckle below yield. How do the two modes differ, and what sets each?
quiz.a: They buckle below yield, but in different modes. In a sandwich the core's low through-thickness stiffness sets a short-wavelength wrinkling mode of the compressed face. A plain sheet of the same thickness buckles globally, over a long wavelength, at a stress set by its own bending stiffness.

quiz.q: A panel has 0.8 mm aluminium faces (E = 70 GPa) on a 15 mm core. Find d and D per metre width.
A floor panel fails by core shear. Suggest two design changes and state what each costs.
quiz.a: Use a denser core or thicker cell walls, which raises shear strength but adds weight and cost. Or increase core thickness, which lowers shear stress for the same load by raising d and D, but takes vertical space and makes local crushing and bolt fixing harder.

quiz.q: Why is a bolt hole through a sandwich panel a problem, and how is it solved?
quiz.a: The bolt bears on the thin faces and crushes the weak core in the through-thickness direction, and clamping can also debond the faces. The hole is potted with a solid insert or filled compound, cured, then drilled so the bolt bears on solid material.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production airframes now fly carbon-fibre faced sandwich panels over Nomex or foam cores, sized by models that treat the core as a thick orthotropic solid rather than as a spring. Research goes into through-thickness reinforcement such as z-pins and stitching to stop debonding. Certification of a bonded panel leans on proof testing, because a weak glue line is hard to see. Search terms: sandwich panel face wrinkling, honeycomb ribbon direction, potted inserts, sandwich flexure test.
